concepts.title: Fitness is an operational responsibility
concepts.explain: A pilot must be mentally and physically capable of safe flight. Meeting a certification standard at one point does not guarantee fitness on a particular day.
concepts.apply: Make an honest preflight self-assessment before accepting responsibility for a flight.

concepts.title: A medical certificate and current health are different
concepts.explain: Medical certification evaluates eligibility under FAA requirements. Symptoms, illness, medications, and fatigue can still make a certificated pilot unfit to fly.
concepts.apply: Do not use the existence of a medical certificate as proof that today is safe.

concepts.title: Aviation medical examiners
concepts.explain: An Aviation Medical Examiner (AME) performs examinations for FAA medical certification. Some medical conditions require additional FAA review.
concepts.apply: Ask an AME or appropriate FAA source about eligibility, rather than guessing from a diagnosis.

concepts.title: BasicMed and other pathways
concepts.explain: Some operations use eligibility paths other than a conventional FAA medical certificate, subject to specific requirements and operating limits.
concepts.apply: Check the current rules for the certificate, operation, and aircraft rather than assuming one medical route fits all.

check.question: You have a valid medical certificate but develop a severe headache before departure. What is the safer choice?
options: Fly because the certificate is valid
Delay flying and evaluate whether you are fit
Only cancel if the weather is bad
check.explanation: A current medical certificate does not override symptoms that could impair safe flight.

concepts.title: What hypoxia means
concepts.explain: Hypoxia occurs when body tissues receive insufficient oxygen. At altitude, reduced oxygen pressure can impair reasoning and coordination before a pilot notices trouble.
concepts.apply: Treat unusual euphoria, confusion, headaches, or degraded performance at altitude as potential warning signs.

concepts.title: Hypoxic hypoxia
concepts.explain: Hypoxic hypoxia arises when insufficient oxygen is available for the blood to absorb, often associated with altitude.
concepts.apply: Know the aircraft oxygen equipment and the applicable operating rules.

concepts.title: Other forms of hypoxia
concepts.explain: Hypemic hypoxia involves inadequate blood oxygen-carrying capacity; stagnant hypoxia involves insufficient circulation; histotoxic hypoxia occurs when tissues cannot properly use oxygen.
concepts.apply: Smoking, some medical problems, and chemical exposures can increase risk.

concepts.title: Time of useful consciousness
concepts.explain: At high altitude, the period during which a pilot can perform purposeful tasks may become very short. The FAA handbook illustrates how time decreases as altitude increases.
concepts.apply: Use oxygen promptly and follow aircraft emergency procedures rather than delaying until symptoms become severe.

concepts.title: Responding to suspected hypoxia
concepts.explain: Follow the aircraft checklist; ensure an appropriate oxygen supply, descend when safe, and obtain medical help as needed.
concepts.apply: Prompt action is essential; an impaired pilot may not reliably judge their own condition.

check.question: A pilot at altitude feels unusually cheerful and starts making simple mistakes. What should be considered?
check.explanation: Euphoria and impaired judgment can be hypoxia symptoms.

concepts.title: Hyperventilation
concepts.explain: Rapid or excessive breathing can reduce carbon dioxide in the blood and cause dizziness, tingling, visual symptoms, and anxiety.
concepts.apply: Symptoms can resemble hypoxia; at altitude, do not assume rapid breathing is harmless.

concepts.title: Responding to rapid breathing
concepts.explain: Use controlled, slower breathing only when appropriate, and address the cause. At altitude, use oxygen and follow procedures for suspected hypoxia.
concepts.apply: Do not rely on a home remedy that could worsen low-oxygen exposure.

concepts.title: Carbon monoxide poisoning
concepts.explain: Carbon monoxide can enter the cockpit through exhaust or heating defects. It prevents effective oxygen delivery and may cause headache, nausea, dizziness, and confusion.
concepts.apply: Treat unexplained symptoms with cabin heat use as a serious hazard.

concepts.title: Suspected exhaust contamination
concepts.explain: Follow the aircraft emergency checklist, shut off suspect cabin heat if applicable, ventilate, use oxygen if available, and land as soon as practical.
concepts.apply: A CO detector can warn of danger, but it does not replace attention to symptoms.

check.question: Headache and dizziness begin after turning on the cabin heater. What is a prudent concern?
check.explanation: A heater or exhaust defect can introduce carbon monoxide into the cockpit.

concepts.title: Pressure changes during climbs and descents
concepts.explain: The middle ear and sinuses contain air spaces that must equalize pressure as altitude changes. Inflammation can interfere with this process.
concepts.apply: Plan conservatively when congested, especially before descending.

concepts.title: Eustachian tube
concepts.explain: The Eustachian tube connects the middle ear with the back of the throat and helps balance pressure across the eardrum.
concepts.apply: Recognize why a cold may make pressure changes painful.

concepts.title: Middle-ear and sinus block
concepts.explain: Trapped pressure can cause pain and hearing or balance problems. Forcing a descent through severe pain can worsen symptoms.
concepts.apply: Follow safe procedures, seek medical guidance, and avoid flight with significant congestion.

concepts.title: Medication is not an automatic solution
concepts.explain: Cold medicines may cause drowsiness or have other side effects, even when they relieve nasal symptoms.
concepts.apply: Assess both the illness and the drug, not just whether breathing feels easier.

check.question: Why can a head cold be a flight risk even when you feel energetic?
options: It can prevent normal ear and sinus pressure equalization
check.explanation: Congestion can block pressure equalization and produce pain or spatial-orientation symptoms.

title: The Inner Ear and Spatial Orientation

concepts.title: How balance works
concepts.explain: The vestibular system in the inner ear senses angular and linear motion. Its signals are useful on the ground but can mislead a pilot in flight.
concepts.apply: Prioritize the flight instruments when outside visual references are unreliable.

concepts.title: Semicircular canals
concepts.explain: Three fluid-filled canals respond to angular acceleration. After a sustained turn, fluid movement changes and a steady turn may no longer feel like a turn.
concepts.apply: Understand why body sensations may conflict with the attitude indicator.

concepts.title: Otolith organs
concepts.explain: The utricle and saccule sense linear acceleration and gravity; in flight, they may interpret acceleration as a change in pitch attitude.
concepts.apply: An acceleration illusion can invite an unsafe nose-down correction.

concepts.title: Why visual reference matters
concepts.explain: A reliable horizon normally helps resolve conflicts between visual and vestibular cues. In clouds or darkness, that reference may disappear.
concepts.apply: If qualified and equipped, use instrument cross-checking rather than the seat-of-the-pants sensation.

check.question: In cloud, the airplane is turning but the pilot feels wings level. Which source is the more reliable attitude reference?
check.explanation: A functioning instrument attitude display is more reliable than vestibular sensation without external references.

concepts.title: The leans
concepts.explain: After an unnoticed slow bank and abrupt correction, the pilot may feel that the aircraft is banking in the opposite direction.
concepts.apply: Resist the urge to re-enter a bank just to satisfy body sensations.

concepts.title: Coriolis illusion
concepts.explain: Rapid head movement during a prolonged turn can stimulate multiple semicircular canals and create a powerful tumbling sensation.
concepts.apply: Minimize unnecessary head movements in instrument conditions and maintain a stable instrument scan.

concepts.title: Graveyard spiral
concepts.explain: A prolonged turn can feel straight. Correcting based on that sensation may lead to renewed bank and tightening descent.
concepts.apply: Use the attitude indicator, heading, and altimeter to identify the actual flight path.

concepts.title: Acceleration and pitch illusions
concepts.explain: Rapid acceleration can feel like pitching up; deceleration can feel like pitching down.
concepts.apply: Cross-check instruments during takeoff, go-around, and other phases with strong acceleration.

concepts.title: False horizons
concepts.explain: Cloud layers, sloping terrain, and nighttime lights may create a false visual horizon.
concepts.apply: Cross-check reliable instruments and avoid trusting a single ambiguous outside cue.

check.question: After prolonged turning in cloud, a pilot feels level but the attitude indicator still shows bank. What is the safe principle?
options: Close the eyes until the sensation passes
check.explanation: Vestibular cues can be misleading during sustained turns.

concepts.title: Runway width illusion
concepts.explain: A narrow runway may appear farther away or higher than expected, tempting a lower-than-normal approach; a wide runway can create the opposite impression.
concepts.apply: Use a stabilized approach and visual approach slope guidance rather than runway width alone.

concepts.title: Runway slope illusion
concepts.explain: An upsloping runway can appear higher than expected; a downsloping runway can appear lower, affecting perceived approach angle.
concepts.apply: Brief runway slope and follow established approach cues.

concepts.title: Featureless terrain illusion
concepts.explain: Approaching over dark water, snow, or unlighted terrain may make the aircraft seem higher than it is.
concepts.apply: Use altitude, descent profile, and available approach lighting.

concepts.title: Atmospheric illusions
concepts.explain: Rain, haze, fog, and bright lights can distort distance and runway perception.
concepts.apply: Avoid changing a stabilized approach solely on the strength of an uncertain visual impression.

concepts.title: Black-hole approaches
concepts.explain: At night, an isolated lit runway without surrounding ground references can encourage an excessively low approach.
concepts.apply: Use suitable vertical guidance when available and discontinue an unstable approach.

check.question: A narrow runway makes the aircraft look high on final. What should a pilot do?
options: Cross-check normal glidepath cues and maintain a stable approach
check.explanation: Runway-width illusion is a known cause of inappropriate glidepath adjustments.

concepts.title: Motion sickness
concepts.explain: Conflicting visual and vestibular signals can cause nausea, dizziness, sweating, and discomfort.
concepts.apply: Focus on the horizon when conditions allow and discuss recurring symptoms with an aviation medical professional.

concepts.title: Anxiety in flight
concepts.explain: Anxiety can narrow attention, alter breathing, and interfere with decision-making.
concepts.apply: Address growing anxiety early instead of allowing it to consume workload capacity.

concepts.title: Stress and performance
concepts.explain: Stress activates the body but excessive or prolonged stress can damage attention and judgment.
concepts.apply: Use a deliberate workload strategy, clear checklists, and a realistic decision to delay or divert.

concepts.title: Personal limitations
concepts.explain: Pilots have different thresholds for stress, distraction, and motion sensitivity.
concepts.apply: Use conservative personal minimums rather than trying to force performance beyond them.

check.question: A passenger becomes airsick and the pilot begins rushing through a checklist. What should be protected first?
options: Aircraft control and safe workload management
Finishing the checklist at maximum speed
check.explanation: Aviate first; manage workload and passengers without compromising aircraft control.

concepts.title: Fatigue affects decisions
concepts.explain: Fatigue can slow reaction time, degrade memory, and reduce vigilance. It may accumulate even without obvious sleepiness.
concepts.apply: Evaluate sleep quality and schedule demands before a flight.

concepts.title: Acute versus cumulative fatigue
concepts.explain: One short night can impair the next day; repeated restricted sleep can create a larger cumulative problem.
concepts.apply: Consider previous nights, not just last night.

concepts.title: Dehydration
concepts.explain: Fluid loss can cause headache, dizziness, tiredness, and reduced alertness, especially in hot cockpits.
concepts.apply: Carry appropriate fluids and manage heat exposure.

concepts.title: Heat stress
concepts.explain: High cockpit temperatures can increase discomfort, fatigue, and cognitive strain.
concepts.apply: Plan cooling, hydration, and conservative departure times when practicable.

concepts.title: Pressure to complete a flight
concepts.explain: Time pressure may tempt a pilot to minimize symptoms or continue despite deteriorating performance.
concepts.apply: Include fatigue and dehydration in your go/no-go assessment.

check.question: Which is a warning sign that should make a pilot reconsider a flight?
options: Repeated poor sleep and difficulty concentrating
check.explanation: Fatigue impairs aeronautical decision-making even when weather and aircraft are acceptable.

concepts.title: Alcohol and flying
concepts.explain: Alcohol impairs judgment, coordination, reaction time, and visual performance. Its effects can persist after the obvious feeling of intoxication has faded.
concepts.apply: FAA regulations set minimum restrictions, but safe decisions may call for longer abstinence.

concepts.title: The regulatory minimum is not a safety target
concepts.explain: Under 14 CFR 91.17, restrictions include operating within eight hours of alcohol consumption, while under the influence, and at or above specified alcohol concentrations.
concepts.apply: Do not treat eight hours as proof that all impairment has disappeared.

concepts.title: Prescription and over-the-counter drugs
concepts.explain: Many medications can affect alertness, vision, balance, or judgment; interactions and side effects may vary.
concepts.apply: Check aviation fitness implications with an AME or qualified aviation medical source.

concepts.title: Supplements and unexpected side effects
concepts.explain: Herbal products and sleep aids may have effects relevant to flying, even if sold without a prescription.
concepts.apply: Test no unfamiliar substance in the cockpit; obtain professional guidance when uncertain.

concepts.title: Illness plus treatment
concepts.explain: Both a medical condition and its medication can impair safe performance.
concepts.apply: A pill that improves one symptom does not automatically restore fitness to fly.

check.question: A pilot is legally past the minimum alcohol waiting interval but still feels hung over. Which decision best supports safety?
options: Fly because the time requirement is satisfied
check.explanation: Regulatory minimums do not override actual fitness or lingering impairment.

concepts.title: Decompression sickness
concepts.explain: Dissolved nitrogen from diving can form bubbles when ambient pressure decreases. Flight at cabin altitudes can increase this risk.
concepts.apply: Avoid rapid altitude exposure after diving.

concepts.title: Wait times depend on dive history
concepts.explain: FAA guidance considers factors including whether a dive required a controlled ascent or decompression stop and the planned flying altitude.
concepts.apply: Use conservative current diving-medicine and FAA guidance for the specific dive profile.

concepts.title: Symptoms of decompression illness
concepts.explain: Joint pain, unusual weakness, sensory changes, dizziness, and other neurological symptoms require prompt medical attention.
concepts.apply: Never assume symptoms after diving are just tiredness.

concepts.title: Cabin pressure still matters
concepts.explain: An aircraft can be pressurized yet still maintain cabin pressure equivalent to an altitude above sea level.
concepts.apply: Do not assume pressurization eliminates decompression risk.

check.question: Why might flying soon after a scuba dive be dangerous?
options: Lower pressure can promote nitrogen bubble formation
check.explanation: A pressure reduction after diving can contribute to decompression sickness.

concepts.title: Central and peripheral vision
concepts.explain: The fovea provides sharp detail and color discrimination; peripheral retina helps detect motion and low light.
concepts.apply: Scan rather than fixate when looking for aircraft.

concepts.title: Rods and cones
concepts.explain: Cones excel in brighter conditions and detail; rods are more sensitive in low light but provide less fine detail and color.
concepts.apply: Understand why night viewing requires different habits.

concepts.title: Blind spot
concepts.explain: Each eye has an optic-disc blind spot where there are no photoreceptors.
concepts.apply: Use a deliberate scanning pattern; one fixed gaze can miss small targets.

concepts.title: Light adaptation
concepts.explain: Eyes adapt to darkness over time, and bright lights can degrade night adaptation.
concepts.apply: Preserve useful cockpit lighting and avoid unnecessary bright-light exposure.

check.question: Which technique helps overcome blind spots and reduced target detection?
options: Hold the eyes still and stare
check.explanation: Systematic scanning moves targets onto sensitive retinal areas.

concepts.title: Night blind spot
concepts.explain: Directly staring at a dim object can make it disappear because central vision is less sensitive in low light.
concepts.apply: Use off-center viewing for dim objects.

concepts.title: Off-center viewing
concepts.explain: Look slightly to one side of a dim object to use more light-sensitive retinal areas.
concepts.apply: Maintain a deliberate, slow scan instead of quickly darting the eyes.

concepts.title: Scanning for traffic
concepts.explain: Divide the outside view into small sectors and pause briefly so each area can be processed.
concepts.apply: Move head and eyes regularly to detect small or stationary-looking traffic.

concepts.title: Relative motion and collision
concepts.explain: Aircraft on a collision course can remain at nearly the same relative bearing while becoming larger in the windscreen.
concepts.apply: A target that does not change bearing may still be closing rapidly.

concepts.title: Night visual discipline
concepts.explain: Reflections, bright cockpit displays, and featureless terrain can reduce visibility and orientation cues.
concepts.apply: Manage lighting and establish clear visual reference or instrument cross-checks.

check.question: A dim light vanishes when you look directly at it. What technique may help?
options: Closing one eye for the rest of the flight
check.explanation: Off-center viewing uses more sensitive areas of the retina under low light.

concepts.title: IMSAFE overview
concepts.explain: IMSAFE is a personal checklist: Illness, Medication, Stress, Alcohol, Fatigue, and Emotion/Eating. It helps structure honest pilot self-assessment.
concepts.apply: Use IMSAFE before every flight, not only when you already feel unwell.

concepts.title: Illness and medication
concepts.explain: Symptoms and treatment both matter for alertness, breathing, pressure equalization, and cognition.
concepts.apply: Consider delaying flight when unwell or affected by drugs.

concepts.title: Stress, fatigue, and emotion
concepts.explain: Distraction, grief, anger, time pressure, and inadequate rest can impair judgment.
concepts.apply: Cancel or adjust plans when personal readiness is below safe standards.

concepts.title: Alcohol and nutrition
concepts.explain: Impairment may remain after minimum legal limits are satisfied; low blood sugar or dehydration can also affect performance.
concepts.apply: Eat and hydrate appropriately and never use regulatory minimums as a measure of readiness.

concepts.title: A personal minimum is actionable
concepts.explain: A useful self-assessment ends with a practical choice: fly, delay, bring help, or cancel.
concepts.apply: Write down personal no-go triggers so you do not negotiate with yourself under pressure.

check.question: You are exhausted, emotionally distracted and otherwise legal to fly. Which IMSAFE principle applies?
options: Personal readiness can justify delaying the flight
IMSAFE matters only for airline pilots
check.explanation: IMSAFE considers personal operational fitness in addition to regulatory eligibility.

concepts.title: Geometric perspective
concepts.explain: Converging lines and relative object size provide clues to distance and position, but can be misleading in unfamiliar environments.
concepts.apply: Verify visual impressions with chart, instrument, and approach information.

concepts.title: Autokinesis
concepts.explain: A fixed, isolated light in darkness may seem to move when stared at.
concepts.apply: Avoid prolonged fixation on a single distant light.

concepts.title: False horizons at night
concepts.explain: Dark land, cloud edges, and isolated lighting can appear to define a horizon when they do not.
concepts.apply: Use appropriate flight instruments and maintain proper instrument proficiency.

concepts.title: Terrain and atmospheric effects
concepts.explain: Haze, uneven lighting, and featureless backgrounds distort perceived distance and height.
concepts.apply: Use a stabilized approach and reliable altitude references.

check.question: A solitary distant light appears to drift as you stare at it. What illusion is possible?
check.explanation: Autokinesis can make an isolated stationary light appear to move.

concepts.title: Start before arriving at the airplane
concepts.explain: Assess sleep, illness, medication, stress, alcohol exposure, hydration, and recent scuba diving.
concepts.apply: The best time to identify a fitness problem is before committing to a departure.

concepts.title: Match risks to flight conditions
concepts.explain: High altitude, night, turbulence, prolonged workload, and challenging approaches increase the impact of aeromedical limitations.
concepts.apply: A tolerable symptom on the ground may become dangerous under flight stress.

concepts.title: Recognize in-flight warning signs
concepts.explain: Headache, confusion, visual changes, disorientation, dizziness, or unusual breathing may signal a serious problem.
concepts.apply: Fly the aircraft, use checklists, take prompt appropriate action, and land when needed.

concepts.title: Know when to ask for assistance
concepts.explain: An AME, flight instructor, medical professional, or ATC can help with different parts of a developing problem.
concepts.apply: Request assistance without delay rather than masking a worsening condition.

concepts.title: Aviation knowledge supports conservative decisions
concepts.explain: Aeromedical education does not diagnose medical conditions or replace professional care.
concepts.apply: Use the handbook as a learning reference and check current FAA requirements for real operations.

check.question: Before a night cross-country, you are congested, sleep-deprived and taking unfamiliar cold medicine. Best decision?
options: Depart because the weather is clear
Delay and evaluate fitness and medication effects
Fly lower so none of these matters
check.explanation: Multiple aeromedical hazards compound risk; a conservative delay is appropriate.
